name: Andaquí
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Coronas Urzúa, Gabriela. 1994. Análisis fonológico de la lengua andaquí. Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 20(1): 69-98. DOI 10.15517/rfl.v20i1.20230 (open access; UCR journal archive PDF)
catalog_locator: p. 97, sec. 10 'Carácter no distributivo del acento' (whole section) and sec. 11 'Conclusiones', third paragraph
catalog_quote: La fuente colonial parece presentar tres acentos: agudo, grave y circunflejo. Sin embargo, este último debe ser más bien indicación de nasalidad vocálica (véase 1.4.3) Albis, por otra parte, sólo incluye los acentos agudo y grave. El acento agudo recae en la posición final, salvo cuatro excepciones. Habría que pensar, por lo tanto, que era fijo en la última sílaba del tema. El acento grave, por otra parte, recae en la sílaba final; parece ser, en consecuencia, un acento fijo en dicha sílaba, por consiguiente, no distintivo. [...] Los diacríticos acento grave y acento agudo representaron probablemente un acento fijo en la última sílaba, que por su condición predecible carecía de valor fonemático.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: The colonial source seems to show three accents: acute, grave and circumflex. However, the latter must rather be an indication of vowel nasality (see 1.4.3); Albis, for his part, only includes the acute and grave accents. The acute accent falls in final position, save four exceptions. One would therefore have to think that it was fixed on the last syllable of the stem. The grave accent, for its part, falls on the final syllable; it seems, consequently, to be an accent fixed on that syllable, and therefore non-distinctive. [...] The grave-accent and acute-accent diacritics probably represented an accent fixed on the last syllable, which, being predictable, lacked phonemic value.
new_statements.citation: Coronas Urzúa, Gabriela. 1994. Análisis fonológico de la lengua andaquí. Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 20(1): 69-98. DOI 10.15517/rfl.v20i1.20230
new_statements.locator: p. 97, sec. 10 'Carácter no distributivo del acento' and sec. 11 'Conclusiones' (PDF page 29 of 30)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (30 pp., text) and rendered p. 29 (printed p. 97) to an image. Sec. 10 'Carácter no distributivo del acento' and the third paragraph of sec. 11 'Conclusiones' are on that page exactly as quoted: 'La fuente colonial parece presentar tres acentos: agudo, grave y circunflejo. Sin embargo, este último debe ser más bien indicación de nasalidad vocálica (véase 1.4.3) Albis, por otra parte, sólo incluye los acentos agudo y grave. El acento agudo recae en la posición final, salvo cuatro excepciones. Habría que pensar, por lo tanto, que era fijo en la última sílaba del tema. El acento grave, por otra parte, recae en la sílaba final; parece ser, en consecuencia, un acento fijo en dicha sílaba,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent fell on the final syllable (of the stem/word) and was predictable, hence non-contrastive; inferred from the placement of acute and grave accent marks in the 18th-century colonial wordlist and Albis's vocabulary.
new_statements.exceptions: Four items in the colonial source carry the acute accent on a non-final syllable (not listed in sec. 10); circumflex marks are reinterpreted as nasality, not accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about written citation forms in colonial-era vocabularies; author says 'última sílaba del tema' (last syllable of the stem) for the acute and 'sílaba final' for the grave, i.e. word/stem-final in isolated word forms. Philological inference from orthographic diacritics, not from speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Extinct language known only from an anonymous 18th-century colonial vocabulary (Real Biblioteca ms.) and Albis (1855/1860-61); Coronas Urzúa's statement is a philological interpretation of the accent diacritics in those written sources, not an observation of speech. Not to be confused with Andaqui as an ethnonym applied to Inga (Quechuan) speakers of the upper Caquetá.

tone_statements.citation: Moens, Jelien & Matthias Pache. 2025. Notes on the grammar of Andakí (Studies in Amerindian Linguistics 2). Berlin: Language Science Press. vi+136 pp. ISBN 978-3-96110-539-7 (digital), 978-3-98554-159-1 (hardcover). DOI 10.5281/zenodo.16964545. [ch. 5 'Phonology' pp. 21-35; sec. 5.2.1 'Suprasegmentals' p. 24; ch. 16 'Concluding summary' p. 111]
tone_statements.quote: Little is known about Andakí suprasegmentals. There is no direct evidence for tone, although the high frequency of homographs in the Andakí sources suggests that lexical tone may have existed in this language. Acute or grave accent is nearly always found in word-final position and may indicate stress, for instance, in <Ypchize canahá quine?> / <Ypchizé canahá quiné?> ‘What did you (sg) bring?’, “Qué has traído?” (M_303); there are no indications for stress being a contrastive feature in Andakí (Coronas Urzúa 1994: 97).
tone_statements.summary: Tone possible but undeterminable from the colonial spellings (homographs hint at unwritten lexical tone); no direct evidence; stress final, non-contrastive.
